state.case_summary:
A 6‐year‐old girl with no relevant medical history presented with intensely pruritic skin lesions on her anterior thighs. The lesions first appeared 2 weeks earlier in recurrent 3‐day outbreaks, always at the same locations, and resolved spontaneously without residual injury. She had no systemic symptoms, preceding infection, topical exposures, sunburn, bites, animal contacts, or recent medications.

On examination, there were well‐defined, confluent, erythematous papules and plaques with annular, arciform, and polycyclic morphology, central clearing, and purpuric edges. Lesions were symmetrically distributed on the anterior thighs in a mirror‐image pattern.

Laboratory studies were within normal limits, including complete blood count, biochemistry, urinalysis, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C‐reactive protein, complement levels (C3, C4, C1q), immunoglobulin levels, rheumatoid factor, and acute‐phase reactants. Antinuclear, anti–double‐stranded DNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, anti–Ro, anti–La, and transglutaminase antibodies were negative. Serologies for syphilis, hepatitis B and C viruses, HIV, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and parvovirus B19 were negative. A chest radiograph was unremarkable.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Urticarial vasculitis
B. Broad differential of annular urticarial lesions in childhood
C. Normal complement and autoantibody studies argue against systemic lupus and other immune‐complex disorders
D. Histopathology confirming leukocytoclastic vasculitis supports urticarial vasculitis
E. Negative direct immunofluorescence makes lupus
F. None
G. None
H. None
